claim.pdf_says: 8.4.3.1.3  Syntax rules  [subordinate to 8.4.3.1 Identifier; a peer of 8.4.3.1.1 General and 8.4.3.1.2 General format]
claim.why_it_matters: A five-component clause number is transcribed at H2, the level the file reserves for two-component clauses such as '## 8.4 References'. The Syntax rules of the identifier clause detach from 8.4.3.1 Identifier in any generated outline.

verdict.reasoning: REFUTED on three independent grounds. (1) The heading is NOT missing. PDF page 156 (printed folio 126) opens with the bold heading '8.4.3.1.3 Syntax rules'. ISO_COBOL.md line 6735 reads '## 8.4.3.1.3 Syntax rules', preceded by an anchor ''. Clause number and title are transcribed verbatim; the only difference is that the PDF's inter-column tab between the number and the title is collapsed to a single space, which is pure whitespace formatting. The 'missing-heading' classification is factually wrong for this page. (2) The claim's stated premise -- that H2 is 'the level the file reserves for two-component clauses' -- is false, and demonstrably so. A tally of all numbered headings in ISO_COBOL.md shows no mapping whatsoever between component count and hash depth: 5-component numbers appear 118 times at '##', 128 times at '###', and 41 times at '####'; 2-component numbers appear 162 times at '##' and 26 times at '###'. The file even carries '### 8.4.1 General' and '### 8.4.2 Uniqueness of reference' at H3 while '## 8.4.3 Identifiers' sits at H2 -- i.e. a child deeper-numbered than its sibling is shallower-hashed. Hash depth in this transcription is not a semantic channel, so no meaning can be read out of it or lost from it. (3) The claim's own local evidence contradicts it. It names 8.4.3.1.1 General and 8.4.3.1.2 General format as unproblematic peers, implying they sit deeper. They do not. Lines 6662/6665/6670/6735 are, in order: '## 8.4.3.1 Identifier', '## 8.4.3.1.1 General', '## 8.4.3.1.2 General format', '## 8.4.3.1.3 Syntax rules'. All four -- parent and all three children -- are at '##'. The flagged heading is at exactly the same level as the two peers cited as correct, so the asserted harm ('detach from 8.4.3.1 Identifier in any generated outline') applies identically to the two headings the claim treats as fine, and to the parent clause itself. Singling out one of four identical rows is not a discrepancy finding. Corroborating check on the source side: I rendered the adjacent page 157 to test whether the PDF encodes clause depth typographically at all. It does not. '8.4.3.1.4 General rules' (5 components), '8.4.3.2 Function-identifier' (4 components), '8.4.3.2.1 General', '8.4.3.2.2 General format' and '8.4.3.2.3 Syntax rules' are all set in the identical bold face, identical point size, and identical left margin with no progressive indentation. Depth is carried solely by the dotted number, which the markdown reproduces exactly. There is therefore no depth signal present in the PDF for the transcription to have dropped. No text is absent, no text is altered, and no meaning changes. This is a markdown nesting convention observation about a global (and globally inconsistent) house style, not a PDF-vs-markdown content discrepancy on page 156.
verdict.corrected_description: Not a discrepancy. The heading '8.4.3.1.3 Syntax rules' is present in ISO_COBOL.md at line 6735, transcribed verbatim from PDF page 156, differing only by collapse of the number/title tab to a single space. The claim's premise that '##' is reserved for two-component clause numbers is false: the file uses '##' for 5-component numbers 118 times, and uses '###'/'####' for 5-component numbers 128/41 times respectively, with no component-count-to-hash-depth mapping anywhere. Within this very clause the parent '## 8.4.3.1 Identifier' and all three children '## 8.4.3.1.1 General', '## 8.4.3.1.2 General format', '## 8.4.3.1.3 Syntax rules' sit at the same '##' level, so the flagged heading is consistent with the peers the claim itself cites as correct. The PDF sets every clause heading at every depth in the same bold face, size and margin (verified on page 157, which shows 8.4.3.1.4, 8.4.3.2, 8.4.3.2.1, 8.4.3.2.2 and 8.4.3.2.3 typographically indistinguishable), so no depth information exists in the source to be lost. If uniform heading-depth normalization is wanted, that is a separate whole-file styling task affecting hundreds of headings, not a page-156 reconciliation finding.
